newsitem.title: UK: Goldsmith - businessman turned maverick politician.
newsitem.headline: Goldsmith - businessman turned maverick politician.

text.p: Anglo-French billionaire businessman Sir James Goldsmith, who died on Saturday aged 64, was a flamboyant corporate raider whose complex business ventures and unorthodox lovelife kept him in the headlines for four decades.

He brought booming self-confidence and a keen sense of timing to every deal that he masterminded in a career that ranged from corporate raider to rightwing politician. He had families, honours and political careers on both sides of the Channel, a seat in the European parliament and an estate in Mexico.

He was married three times and fathered three sons and three daughters. In the 1990s he used his fortune, estimated at billions of dollars, to campaign against what he saw as the threat of a European superstate.

Goldsmith's investment motto was: "If you see a bandwagon, it's too late." Such was his touch that in the 1970s and 1980s even a casual expresssion of his interest in a company was enough to send its share price soaring.

A tall man with striking blue eyes, Goldsmith was never afraid to take chances, in life or business. At 20 he eloped with Isabel Patino, daughter of a Bolivian tin mining magnate and married her despite fierce opposition from her family.
James Michael Goldsmith was born in Paris on February 26, 1933 into an old European banking family of an Anglo-Jewish father and a French Catholic mother.
His father was a Conservative member of parliament in Britain for eight years but was hounded out by anti-semitism during World War One.

Goldsmith attended Britain's elite Eton school. He left without a single qualification, but started his business career in his late teens, when he sold electrical plugs and pharmaceutical products in France.
It took off when he was 20, when he bought the rights to a British rheumatism cream for 100 pounds and sold them three years later for 250,000 pounds.
He almost went bankrupt in 1957 but was reprieved by a French bank strike, which provided a convenient excuse to fend off the creditors lining up to demand payment.
He sold the business and returned to London to develop a group of shops catering for mothers and babies.
Operating smoothly between Britain and France, his next big success was Milical, a slimming aid that eventually sold throughout Europe.
By the start of the 1970s he had the funds to back real money-making ventures -- taking over and dismembering firms to make them more efficient, or, for critics, asset-stripping.

Bovril was one of the better-known names acquired, but Goldsmith also moved into biscuits, chocolate and slimming foods. His Cavenham Food group eventually became the world's third-largest food company.
There were some failures along the way, notably the glossy current affairs magazine Now!, launched in 1979 but dead by mid-1981.

Goldsmith was a frequent target of the satirical British Private Eye magazine, reaching a low point in 1976 when he filed 63 libel writs against the magazine, which ridiculed the food magnate as "Sir Jams".
He also financed libel suits filed by other, less well-heeled public figures as a matter of principle.
He built up a big stake in Britain's Express Newspapers in the 1970s, but never managed to achieve control. Inevitably he made a big profit when he sold out.

He had more luck with the French media, controlling the right-of-centre news magazine, L'Express, in the 1980s and turning it into a vehicle of opposition to the ruling Socialists after their 1981 election victory.
In 1980, Goldsmith turned his attention to the United States.

His first target was Diamond International, a 100-year-old pulp and paper maker which he acquired for $750 million in 1982. Three years later, he bought timber and distribution firm Crown Zellerbach for $1.5 billion, selling much of it on for a profit.
A massive 1989 bid for Anglo-U.S. tobacco and financial services firm B.A.T Industries foundered in the U.S. courts.
But it was his 1986 raid on the Goodyear Tire and Rubber Company, the world's top tyre-maker, that made Goldsmith notorious in the United States.

Goodyear chairman Robert Mercer accused him of being "obsessed with pursuing his targets" and Goldsmith, who believed Goodyear should shed its peripheral businesses and focus on its tyre operations, was labelled a threat to American workers.
"Who the hell are you?" he was asked by Representative John Seiberling, the grandson of Goodyear's founder, during Congressional hearings on takeovers.
The question highlighted Goldsmith's mysterious background. "The English say he's not English, the French say he's not French and the Americans know he's not American," an old friend said.
Goldsmith walked away with more than $90 million in profits after selling his stake back to the company.

The October 1987 global stock market crash barely touched him -- he had sold all but a five per cent stake in Paris-listed Generale Occidentale, the holding company for his European interests, for an estimated $450 million shortly before.

In the 1990s he turned increasingly to politics, and ruffled establishment feathers in that field, too. His daughter Jemima married former Pakistan cricketer-turned-politician Imran Khan and helped him in his unsuccessful election campaign in 1997.
Instinctively right-wing, Goldsmith was also an industrialist who put money into environmental causes, and an international businessman who believed free trade is dangerous.
He was European in outlook and won a French seat in the Strasbourg European parliament, but was strongly opposed to a European super-state in which nations would lose their identity.

In 1994, he founded a British political party -- the Referendum Party -- to campaign for a free vote on Britain's integration in Europe, and spent some 20 million pounds of his own money on the campaign for the 1996 general election.

His party failed to win any seats but polled a respectable 812,000 votes. Goldsmith himself, already suffering from a recurrence of pancreatic cancer, won only 1,500 votes in the London constituency of Putney.
The last picture most Britons saw of him was on election night when he broke into an unseemly chant of "Out! Out!" against the defeated Conservative candidate after the election result was announced.
He was given a knighthood by Britain in 1976 and made a knight of the Legion of Honour by France in 1978.
He never cared much for what the establishment thought, his complicated love life being the best example.
His elopement with Patino ended tragically when she died within months, but the baby she was carrying was saved.

During his second marriage to Frenchwoman Ginette Lery, Goldsmith openly kept an aristocratic mistress in London, Lady Annabel Vane Tempest Stewart, marrying her after his marriage to Lery was dissolved.
But by the 1990s, there was already a third woman in his life, Laure Boulay de la Meurthe, with whom he shared his 18,000-acre estate in Mexico and his home in Paris.
